title: The lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22–24)
hookLine: the eye is the lamp; you can't serve God and mammon

lines: SOONER OR LATER, YOU PICK ONE.
cards: Try working for two bosses at once. One wants the report by noon; the other wants you at a meeting at noon. One says cut costs; the other says spend.
Sooner or later you pick one, and the other one notices. Two jobs, or two households with different rules, work the same way. Jesus has two pictures for it: a lamp, and a servant with two masters.

teach.b: First, the lamp. In the King James Bible: "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light."
Single translates a Greek word that can mean simple, undivided, and also generous. In Jewish idiom, a good eye meant a generous person, and an evil eye a stingy one.
Proverbs says the one with a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he gives his bread to the poor. So a single eye looks at the world openly and generously, and the whole person fills with light.

teach.h: NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.
teach.b: Then the second picture: "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
Serve here means serve as a slave, not a part-time job, and a slave can't belong fully to two owners.
Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth or property, the stuff you own and rely on. Some scholars think it comes from a root meaning that in which you trust, though nobody is sure.

teach.h: YE CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.
teach.b: It wasn't the name of a god; medieval writers later turned Mammon into a demon, and the poet Milton put him in Paradise Lost.
But Jesus uses it almost like a person, a rival master, because that's how money can act: it makes demands, it promises safety, it asks for your time and your worry.
Look back at this week: the other cheek, love for enemies, giving in secret, few words, our Father, moths and rust, and now one master. Each asks: who, finally, do you belong to?

how: Christians often speak of stewardship, holding money as something entrusted by God, and some practice regular giving, simple living or fasting from spending as ways to keep money a servant rather than a master.

games.q: you're trying to serve God and money equally, giving each a fair share of your heart. what does Jesus say?
o: no one can serve two masters.
games.why: "No man can serve two masters ... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." sooner or later, you hold to one.

practice: Think back over today: where did your eyes keep landing? Price tags, other people's things, your balance, a face you love; no verdict, just notice.
Then picture your eye as a lamp and ask what today would look like through a generous eye, and if you pray, ask for a single eye.

wordCard.voice: Mammon. Aramaic for wealth, the things you own and trust; Jesus names it as a rival master. You can't serve both.

orig.note: Greek spelling of an Aramaic word: wealth, property. Matthew 6:24.

carryVoice: Your line: one master. A single eye fills the whole body with light. And that's a week.
